summary: Defines a TCP option that lets one end of a connection tell the other its user timeout, which is how long sent data may stay unacknowledged before the connection is forcibly closed. Normally that value is only local to each side, so sharing it lets peers coordinate.

eli5.summary: If you call a friend and hear nothing, you decide how long to wait before hanging up. This note lets each side of a TCP connection tell the other how long it is willing to wait.

questions: what is the tcp user timeout option
how long does tcp wait before closing a connection
how does tcp user timeout affect keep-alives
subtitle: A TCP option that lets each end tell the other how long it will wait for acknowledgments before giving up.

tldr.problem: TCP's user timeout, how long sent data may go unacknowledged before the connection is closed, is purely local, so one side raising it does not stop the other side from closing the connection.
tldr.mechanism: The TCP User Timeout Option (kind 28, 4 bytes) carries a 15-bit timeout in seconds or minutes, and the receiver may adopt it as advice within its own upper and lower limits.
tldr.outcome: Both ends can agree to survive longer outages, or a busy server can warn clients it will keep state only briefly. The option is advisory, and long timeouts raise resource-exhaustion risks.

today: RFC 5482 is a Proposed Standard from March 2009, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The option is advisory, so a TCP may ignore the advice if local policy says so.

sections.title: Why Share the User Timeout
sections.content:
The TCP specification (RFC 793) defines a local, per-connection user timeout: the maximum time transmitted data may remain unacknowledged before TCP forcefully closes the connection. Without an application-specified value, RFC 793 sets a default of 5 minutes. RFC 1122 adds thresholds R1 and R2 for retransmission attempts.

TCP has no way to tell the other end about a changed user timeout. A local increase does not help a connection survive a long outage, because the other end still closes it when its own timeout expires. RFC 5482 fixes this with the TCP User Timeout Option (UTO).

The RFC names scenarios that benefit: mobile hosts that are only intermittently connected, transient disruptions from congestion or link or routing failures, and predictable outages such as a node in space losing line of sight behind a planet.
sections.eli5: If you decide to wait a long time on the phone but your friend hangs up after a minute, your patience does not matter. This option lets you tell your friend how long you can wait.

sections.title: How the Option Is Used
sections.content:
TCP keeps four per-connection variables. USER_TIMEOUT is the existing parameter. The new ones are ADV_UTO (the value advertised to the peer, defaulting to the system-wide user timeout), ENABLED (default false, applies to sending and receiving) and CHANGEABLE (default true, and it becomes false when an application explicitly sets USER_TIMEOUT).

The exchange is not a binding negotiation. A UTO option is a suggestion, and the receiver adapts only if both ENABLED and CHANGEABLE are true. Setting these before an active or passive open puts UTO options in the SYN and SYN-ACK segments. A connection that has enabled UTO SHOULD also include one in the first packet without the SYN flag, which helps when SYN cookies are used. A host SHOULD include the option in the next outgoing segment whenever it starts using a new user timeout.

A TCP that does not support the option MUST silently ignore it. TCP option space is limited to 40 bytes, so other options may already use it all.
sections.eli5: Each side holds up a card saying how long it will wait. The other side may copy it, but only if it has said that is okay.

sections.title: Choosing the New Timeout
sections.content:
If CHANGEABLE is false, USER_TIMEOUT MUST NOT change, though TCP SHOULD tell the application the received value. Otherwise hosts SHOULD adjust it. Implementations MUST impose limits on the values they accept. Under the RECOMMENDED scheme:

USER_TIMEOUT = min(U_LIMIT, max(ADV_UTO, REMOTE_UTO, L_LIMIT))

The result is the larger of the two advertised values, kept between the local upper limit (U_LIMIT) and lower limit (L_LIMIT). The two ends will not necessarily adopt the same timeout. The end that advertised the smaller value can still close or abort whenever it wants.

The lower limit SHOULD be at least 100 seconds, and it MUST be larger than the connection's current retransmission timeout (RTO), or the connection could be aborted needlessly. The upper limit reduces the effect of resource exhaustion attacks. Limits may be system-wide or per host, user, interface or connection, and may change with resource use or attack status.

Very short values can hurt transmissions over high-delay paths. Long ones make hosts keep connection state for a long time.
sections.eli5: Both sides look at the two waiting times, pick the longer one, and then make sure it is not too short or too long for their own rules.

sections.title: The Option Format
sections.content:
The option is 4 bytes long. Kind MUST be 28 and Length MUST be 4. The G (granularity) bit says how to read the 15-bit User Timeout field: when G is 1 the value is in minutes, and when G is 0 it is in seconds.

That lets hosts exchange timeouts from 1 second to over 9 hours in seconds, and from 1 minute to over 22 days in minutes. The value applies to the synchronized states (ESTABLISHED, FIN-WAIT-1, FIN-WAIT-2, CLOSE-WAIT, CLOSING, LAST-ACK). Connections in other states MUST use the default timeouts from RFC 793 and RFC 1122.

A User Timeout of zero, with G of either 0 or 1, is reserved. Current implementations MUST NOT send it and MUST ignore it on reception.

The option is advisory and need not be delivered reliably, and no reliability handshake is defined. Implementations MAY retransmit it with the segment that carried it, but MUST NOT assume it arrives.
sections.eli5: It is a tiny note with a number and a switch. The switch says whether the number means seconds or minutes.

sections.title: Middleboxes and Keep-Alives
sections.content:
Because unknown options MUST be silently ignored, the RFC adds no negotiation during the three-way handshake. It cites a study in which 3% of connections failed when an unknown option appeared in the middle of a connection, and judges that too few to need special measures. Implementations may send UTO on the first data segments to detect a problem middlebox. If segments carrying it are persistently lost, they should turn UTO off for that connection. Stateful firewalls may still close idle connections whatever the option says.

Some TCP implementations, such as in BSD systems, use a different abort policy for keep-alives. If keep-alives and UTO are both used, the keep-alive timer MUST be larger than the adopted USER TIMEOUT.

The RFC also expects TCP implementations to extend their APIs, and expects the TCP MIB documents to add objects for UTO later.
sections.eli5: Some old devices on the path might get confused by an unfamiliar note, but they should just ignore it. Keep-alive pings must not give up sooner than the agreed waiting time.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Longer timeouts make resource exhaustion easier: a server must keep state for throw-away connections for longer. TCP does not become more vulnerable to simple SYN flooding, because UTO values affect only synchronized states, which simple SYN floods never reach. An attacker who completes handshakes can make the effect worse.

Mitigations in the RFC:

  • Require prior peer authentication, such as IPsec or TCP-MD5, or in-band authentication such as a completed TLS handshake, before accepting long timeouts.
  • Apply a per-peer limit on the number of connections with increased timeouts.
  • Reduce accepted timeouts as resource use rises, since per-peer limits do not stop distributed attacks.
  • Use trust level when shedding load by resetting connections.
  • Apply the upper and lower limits from the previous sections.

Connections reset to shed load are no worse off than without the option.
sections.eli5: If everyone asks you to hold their place in line for hours, your line could fill up. So you can limit how long you wait, and say no to strangers.
